lines: Riley Chen
+1 (555) 010-7731 | riley.chen@example.com | example.com/in/riley-chen
EDUCATION
Northfield School of Management | MBA | Metro City, USA | Sep 2023 - Jun 2025
Lakeview University | B.A. in Economics | Lake City, USA | Sep 2014 - Jun 2018
EXPERIENCE
Coastal Marine Services | Diesel Mechanic | Lake City, USA | Jul 2025 - Present
- Rebuilt diesel engines and gearboxes for a fleet of 14 commercial fishing vessels, keeping dry-dock time under 5 days per job.
- Maintained hydraulic winch systems and logged service records for the harbor authority's annual inspections.
Crestline Logistics | Operations Analyst | Lake City, USA | Jul 2018 - Aug 2023
- Owned the weekly carrier scorecards for the regional managers and the monthly review meeting that discussed them.
- Cut warehouse pick errors 30% at two sites by redesigning slotting rules with the floor supervisors and retraining 45 pickers on the new layout.
- Ran the quarterly S&OP review across sales, finance and operations for 12 consecutive quarters, introducing a consensus forecast that cut forecast error from 18% to 11%.

- Led the rollout of a route-planning tool to 3 depots while rewriting the standard operating procedures, running driver training and taking over vendor negotiations for the telematics contract, which saved 1,800 driver hours a year across the region.
Harbor Payments | Associate Product Manager Intern | Metro City, USA | Jun 2024 - Aug 2024
- Redesigned merchant onboarding around a single verification step, cutting median time to first payment from 9 days to 4 across 2,300 new merchants in the pilot region.
- Lifted checkout conversion from 61% to 66% by testing a one-page flow against the three-step flow across 40,000 sessions, then shipping it to all merchants.
- Prioritized the dispute roadmap with RICE, scoring Reach as the number of support tickets each feature would close.
- After interviewing 25 merchants, mapping chargeback reasons, sizing the loss by segment and drafting a business case with finance, set the next quarter's roadmap priority.
- Ran the checkout A/B test with randomization by session and reported the 5-point conversion lift as the effect on merchants' customers.
- Presented the onboarding results and a follow-up roadmap to the payments leadership team, who funded the rollout to two more regions.
PROJECTS
Campus Food Rescue App | Product Lead | Student Venture | Oct 2023 - Present
- Launched a surplus-food pickup app to 3,100 students with two dining halls, redistributing 9 tonnes of food that would have been thrown away in its first year.
- Raised weekly active users from 400 to 1,150, a 150% increase, by adding pickup reminders chosen after 60 user interviews.
- Raised the pickup-slot fill rate by 20% across two dining halls, from 75% to 95%, by setting up a volunteer shift system.
MBA Consulting Practicum | Team Lead | Regional Hospital Network | Jan 2024 - May 2024
- Sized a $2.4M annual saving from consolidating outpatient scheduling across 4 clinics; the client funded a pilot based on the model.
- Patient intake at 4 clinics was mapped and the intake form was shortened, with the changes adopted by front-desk staff.
- Presented the final recommendation to the hospital COO and clinic directors, who approved a 90-day scheduling pilot at two clinics.
SKILLS
Product: roadmapping, A/B testing, user interviews, requirements writing
Tools: Jira, Amplitude, Excel

items.says: The experience order is not newest-first, and the current sequence places the diesel-mechanic role after the MBA in a way that makes the career direction appear to move backward.
items.because: A product or operations reader may therefore miss the intended product/operations progression and question the narrative after the MBA.

items.says: Projects should appear before Education if product management is the target.
items.because: The product internship and student product work are stronger evidence of the target direction than the academic history.

items.says: The dry-dock result has no comparison showing whether under five days was an improvement, a standard, or the normal turnaround.
items.because: The reader can see the achieved speed but cannot judge its significance.

items.says: The line says the hydraulic winch systems were maintained but does not show either the technical work performed or its operational result.
items.because: "Maintained" could mean inspection, troubleshooting, repair, adjustment, or replacement, so the reader cannot identify the hands-on skill demonstrated.

items.says: The carrier-scorecard bullet gives responsibility and meeting cadence but no result or clear operating mechanism.
items.because: A hiring manager can see that scorecards were weekly and the review was monthly, but not whether the work improved carrier performance, service, cost, or decisions.

items.says: The S&OP bullet uses unexplained jargon and places the forecast improvement after the meeting and process context.
items.because: Readers outside supply-chain planning may not know that S&OP means sales and operations planning.

items.says: The route-planning bullet buries the 1,800-hour result after too many actions and does not show its comparison point.
items.because: The savings appears only after rollout, SOP rewriting, training, and vendor negotiations, so a scanning reader may miss the strongest evidence.

items.says: The line implies that 40,000 sessions alone justified shipping the flow to all merchants.
items.because: Session volume does not establish randomization, statistical reliability, acceptable guardrail metrics, or representativeness of all merchants.

items.says: The phrase "shipping it" has an ambiguous antecedent because the sentence discusses both the flow and the test.
items.because: A scanning reader may not know whether "it" refers to the one-page flow or the experiment.

items.says: The RICE line defines Reach incorrectly as raw support-ticket volume rather than the number of unique affected users, customers, or accounts.
items.because: Standard RICE Reach estimates how many unique users, customers, or accounts are affected during a defined period.

items.says: The RICE prioritization bullet gives neither the resulting roadmap change nor a comparison from the scoring.
items.because: The reader sees a method but not what decision it produced or why one feature ranked ahead of another.

items.says: The phrase "sizing the loss by segment" gives no loss estimate or segment comparison and uses internal jargon.
items.because: The method is visible, but the reader cannot see what the analysis established or why one segment mattered more.

items.says: The dispute-roadmap bullet ends with a decision but does not identify the priority or expected value.
items.because: The reader cannot tell what the research and business case changed or which problem the next quarter would address.

items.says: The process list buries the roadmap decision under four research and business-case activities.
items.because: A scanning reader may miss the product outcome because the main decision appears only after the methods.

items.says: The line calls the 61%-to-66% movement a 5-point lift without specifying that it is a percentage-point lift.
items.because: The metric moved by five percentage points, not by 5 percent.

items.says: The checkout result is described as a session-level experiment but then reported as an effect on merchants' customers.
items.because: Randomization by session supports a session-level conversion effect, not automatically an effect on unique customers.

items.says: The funding bullet does not identify which onboarding result supported the rollout decision.
items.because: Leadership funding is a strong outcome, but the reader cannot connect it to a specific measured improvement.

items.says: The wording makes the funding outcome grammatically dependent on the leadership team instead of emphasizing what the presentation secured.
items.because: The current construction foregrounds who funded the rollout rather than the candidate's role in obtaining approval.

items.says: The two checkout-testing bullets repeat the same A/B test and five-point improvement.
items.because: Repeating the experiment makes the internship read like a task list and uses space that could show another product decision or technical detail.

items.says: The two dispute-roadmap bullets repeat the same prioritization work while separating its research, sizing, method, and decision.
items.because: The duplication makes the work look fragmented and leaves the reader to assemble one product decision from two bullets.

items.says: The app's launch scope is ambiguous, and the phrase about food that would have been discarded makes an unsupported counterfactual claim.
items.because: Recording 9 tonnes collected through the app does not prove that all of it would otherwise have been thrown away.

items.says: The launch bullet shows the outcome but not the product or operating method that produced it.
items.because: A reader can see that 9 tonnes were redistributed, but cannot tell what product-lead contribution made the result possible.

items.says: The stated 150% increase is arithmetically wrong: growth from 400 to 1,150 is a 187.5% increase.
items.because: The percentage increase is (1,150 − 400) ÷ 400 × 100, which equals 187.5%.

items.says: The rise in weekly active users is attributed entirely to pickup reminders without evidence that the reminders caused it.
items.because: The 60 interviews support how the feature was selected, but they do not establish causation for the movement from 400 to 1,150.

items.says: The phrase "chosen after 60 user interviews" does not clearly explain what the interviews informed.
items.because: A reader can tell interviews happened, but not whether they selected the reminder concept, its content, timing, or another feature detail.

items.says: The line incorrectly describes the change from 75% to 95% as a 20% increase instead of a 20-percentage-point increase.
items.because: The endpoints show a 20-percentage-point change, while the relative increase is approximately 26.7%.

items.says: The volunteer-shift method is too generic to show how it improved pickup-slot fill.
items.because: The result moves from 75% to 95%, but the reader cannot see what the shift system changed operationally.

items.says: The $2.4M annual-saving estimate lacks the cost or operating baseline against which it was measured.
items.because: The figure shows a large opportunity, but the reader cannot quickly tell how it was calculated or what current cost it represents.

items.says: The phrase "based on the model" is vague about how the client used the analysis.
items.because: The client funded a pilot, but the reader cannot tell whether the model supported approval, prioritization, design, or another decision.

items.says: The intake-process bullet gives no resulting improvement and does not quantify how much the form was shortened.
items.because: Adoption by front-desk staff proves acceptance, not whether the change reduced effort, time, errors, or patient friction.

items.says: The phrase "final recommendation" is generic and does not identify the analysis or subject behind it.
items.because: The reader sees senior-stakeholder exposure but not the consulting skill that supported the recommendation.

items.says: The practicum repeats the scheduling-pilot approval in two bullets instead of presenting the savings estimate and approval as one result.
items.because: Both bullets report that the client approved or funded a scheduling pilot, so the repetition spends space without adding evidence.
